Whups, I didn't read all of your comment before replying. My bad.

Just for reference though, I do much prefer using a paper wallet, and sweeping it into a client rather than just importing. Reduces UTXOs that way.

Multidoge is a 'lite' wallet client. It doesn't download the entire blockchain, only the bits it needs.

Lite wallets are really really bad things when there are a lot of transactions. That's why they warn you not to use them for mining (or faucets). Or, in fact, anything that generates a pile of UTXOs. Because the coins will basically become unspendable.

Fortunately, there is an answer.

First, look up each wallet address on the blockchain, with whatever your favourite explorer is. I like bitinfocharts.com, though it doesn't work on OSX 10.5 :(

Take not of wallets with lots of Unspent Transactions, UTXOs. That's the difference between inputs and outputs. So 200 in and 100 out means 100 UTXOs in the wallet. Anything over about a hundred is a problem. Thousands guarantee you'll kill the client and won't be able to spend them.

You need to extract the private key(s) for the affected wallet(s). I don't use Multidoge, so I can't offer guidance on how, but poke around a bit and you should find it.

Once you have a private key, you'll need a sweeper service and a wallet to sweep the coins into.

You can generate as many wallets as you need with a paper wallet generator. I have one on my page at http://fulvio55.altervista.org that does about 80 currencies. Just generate a bunch of bulk keys (be sure you're offline if you're paranoid, but the Mac is more robust than PC's, so you should be safe enough from malware). Be sure to make backups of whatever file you store them in, and print a copy or two for good measure. There's no need for the fancy wallets with the QR codes and all.. you just need the keys.

There are a few sweeping services out there. Dogechain.info and Redeempaper.com are two that work well. Input your private key, then the public key of the wallet you want the coins to go to. Assuming there aren't so many that you crash the browser (the code runs in your browser, not on the remote service), after a few seconds the coins will be gone and you'll have a transaction ID. If you open it, you will see lots of inputs, but only one output, in the new address.

Congratulations, you've now eradicated a whole mess of those nasty UTXOs that are really bad for the network.

If you plan it right, you can use sets of cascading wallets to consolidate coins quite efficiently. After the weekend blackout's over, you can read my posts on the subject on Reddit, or in the meantime, here's a pic showing three cascading wallets. Note how many transactions were in the first one, from before I knew better. http://www.bitpixr.com/i/cascading-paper-wallets/

Good luck, and if you need more help, just ask. I'll be here all weekend. :)

As I said, there's no need for it to be physical paper, as such.

A wallet is just a number. A 256-bit key, with a type ID and a checksum added. That's all it is, whether its in a client, in a text file, on a bit of paper or carved into a tree.

I keep all my wallets in a plain text file, and when I need one, I just copy the key, sweep the coins to QT or an online wallet or wherever. Easy. I even do that with wallets that are in QT, to minimise fees.

Easiest way to get the hang of it is to try. Grab the generator, run off a dozen keys, send 100 coins to one, and try moving it around.

Also, you will want another file with a list of ALL your wallets, no matter where they are. I use a HTML file, coded by hand to keep it simple. Each wallet has a link to a blockchain explorer, like so: https://bitinfocharts.com/dogecoin/address/D5fQ9cov3FbSESewm83ZUgvdy1bSCFLSQ4 which is one of the donation addresses for the #DogeV8 project.

Here's a shortened sample of my actual file, but with fake addresses. The V8 wallets are real though:

http://fulvio55.altervista.org/test/sample.html

Note that each service has a pair of wallets, Fr/To. That is, there is the address of the service's online wallet, be it an exchange, tipbot or whatever, and a matching receive address for withdrawals from the service. Because the blockhain is a permanent record of every transaction ever made, if you have multiple inputs in a transaction, they must have come from the same source, and therefore can be identified as belonging to the same person and traced. Not good for privacy, so keep the relationships 1:1 as much as possible.
